name: Canine fossa theory

lead: The canine fossa is a shallow depression on the front of the upper jaw, below the cheekbone and beside the canine tooth. In looksmaxxing discussions, the canine fossa theory proposes that how deep or recessed this hollow is, together with midface bone structure, helps determine whether the cheeks look hollow and defined beneath the cheekbones.

People use the idea to explain differences in cheek hollowing between faces and to decide whether leanness, bone structure or both matter for a defined cheek. The anatomy of the fossa is well documented in medical literature, but the link to cheek appearance is a community hypothesis that published studies have not tested.

paras: In practice the theory is a way of looking at a face: members compare photos or CT skull images, note how recessed the area below the cheekbone appears, and discuss whether a lean face or a skeletal difference explains cheek hollows. Discussions around it commonly mention lowering body fat, midface and maxillary development, and, in some threads, surgical or filler options for volume.

The theory itself is not a procedure. Procedures discussed alongside it, such as midface implants or fat reduction methods, carry their own risks; surgery in this region can involve nerve branches of the face, which anatomical studies have mapped because of operations on the maxillary sinus.

angle.text: Followers of the theory use it to interpret cheek hollows: a deeper or more recessed fossa is said to contribute to hollowing, while leanness reveals it. They use it to decide whether fat loss, bone structure or both explain a cheek contour.

lead: The canine fossa is a depression on the outer surface of the maxilla, the upper jaw bone. It sits beside the smaller incisive fossa, is separated from it by a ridge called the canine eminence, and is the origin of the levator anguli oris muscle that lifts the corner of the mouth.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing communities, the canine fossa theory holds that the depth of this fossa, together with the overall development of the maxilla, contributes to hollow cheeks, the visible shadowed area under the cheekbones that many forum members regard as an attractive trait. People use it to explain why some faces show hollowing at relatively higher body fat while others do not, and to weigh leanness against bone structure.[3][4]

Medical literature on the canine fossa concerns anatomy, sinus surgery and midface implants rather than cheek aesthetics. Surgeons use it as an entry point for the maxillary sinus, and a device called the Maxout implant was designed to add volume at the canine fossa for midface rejuvenation.[5][6]

Cheek hollowness is also discussed in the clinical aesthetic literature. A 2024 narrative review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open describes an ideal cheek contour called the ogee curve, a concave arc flowing into a convex one, and notes that midface volume loss, maxillary recession and weakening of retaining ligaments change how hollow the cheek looks.[7] The review's authors have commercial ties to filler makers, which readers may wish to weigh.[7]

paras: The canine fossa is larger and deeper than the incisive fossa and lies lateral to the canine eminence, which overlies the root of the canine tooth; the levator anguli oris arises from it.[1] A descriptive reference text states that it lies below the infraorbital foramen and that its dimensions vary between individuals and with bone resorption after tooth loss.[2]

Its anterior-wall location over the maxillary sinus is why it appears frequently in surgical literature: a puncture or incision through it gives access for sinus procedures, and studies have mapped nerve branches in the region and the incidence of complications such as cheek numbness or facial nerve branch weakness.[8][9][10]

The fossa itself has been described in anatomical texts for over a century; Wikipedia's entry cites Gray's Anatomy (1918) for its location and muscle attachment.[1] The looksmaxxing framework built on it appears in several looksmax.org threads, including ones titled as guides to how hollow cheeks work, to the 'two types' of hollow cheeks, and one in which the poster argues against the theory, showing that the idea is debated within the community.[11][12][13]

Threads on hollow cheeks and the fossa are usually posted alongside photo ratings and skull comparisons, and they feed into a wider vocabulary of midface terms such as maxilla development, midface projection and cheekbone prominence. The theory has not been associated with a named originator or with coverage in mainstream media or influencer channels that this wiki could verify.

On looksmax.org, threads on hollow cheeks discuss the fossa as one factor. One thread argues that visible bone structure is a positive when the face is lean, while another contributor suggests that very hollow cheeks can look gaunt and that dimples can show bone without that effect.[3]

Another thread proposes a hypothesis that a recessed canine fossa and midface correlate with a tendency toward facial redness or rosacea, supported by skull CT comparisons; the poster presents it as a personal hypothesis.[4] Other threads on the topic cover fat loss and diet for hollow cheeks, and the debate over whether the fossa matters or whether leanness alone produces the look.[14]

Surgeons distinguish several causes of a hollow cheek. Plastic surgeon Barry Eppley writes that youthful, isolated hollow cheeks can be attractive, whereas hollowing that accompanies age-related facial fat loss is not, and that the amount of bony prominence around the cheek strongly affects how hollowing is perceived.[15] The 2024 review describes the midface as one of the first areas to show ageing, with deep medial and buccal fat shrinking and nasolabial folds deepening, and notes that hyaluronic acid fillers are used to restore midface volume.[7]

The buccal fat pad, a deep fat mass between the buccinator and masseter, is linked in Wikipedia's summary to hollow cheeks and the nasolabial fold; its removal (buccal fat extraction) is sometimes used to reduce cheek prominence, and the same article notes a significant risk to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct.[16] This soft-tissue route is distinct from the bone-based canine fossa explanation, and forum discussions commonly weigh the two, along with overall body fat, when explaining why people differ in cheek hollowing.[2][4]

A controlled clinical series described the Maxout implant, a transmaxillary implant configured to add height at the canine fossa for midface volume replacement in people requesting midface augmentation.[5]

Reviews of canine fossa puncture techniques in endoscopic sinus surgery report complications and describe landmarks to reduce them, indicating that surgery in the region involves facial sensory nerves.[8][9]

No studies found that test whether canine fossa depth influences cheek hollowing or rosacea. Related surgical studies cover canine fossa puncture in sinus surgery, including randomized comparisons in chronic sinusitis, and one controlled series of a midface implant at the fossa.[5][10][17]

timeline.event: Gray's Anatomy describes the canine fossa and its levator anguli oris origin, the text cited by Wikipedia.[1]
A review of Caldwell-Luc indications describes the maxillary sinus approach through the canine fossa.[6]
The Maxout transmaxillary implant for midface volume is described; a cadaver study maps anterior maxilla innervation for canine fossa puncture.[5][9]
Case reports and trials examine buccal branch weakness and canine fossa puncture in chronic sinusitis.[10][17]
A review of facial contour and volume correction discusses the ogee curve and midface hollowing; looksmax.org threads on hollow cheeks and the fossa continue.[3][4][7]
